introduction-the-developers-overflowing-.core: In 2010 a developer needed Java and SQL. Now they're also expected to know containers, Kubernetes, CI/CD, IaC, cloud IAM, observability and security. The 'you build it, you run it' shift overflowed cognitive capacity, and Team Topologies plus platforms rebalance it.

first_principles.problem: Developers are overwhelmed by the infrastructure they're expected to master, and delivery slows while burnout rises.
derivation: Define **interaction modes**; start with a **TVP**; **measure** load.

analogy.title: A chef who must also be the plumber and electrician
analogy.story: Cooking quality falls when the chef keeps fixing the building.
analogy.breaks: Developers still need some operational knowledge to own production well.

branches.label: Cause
children: You build it, you run it

example.title: Alex's stack, 2010 vs today
flow: Today: + Docker, K8s, Helm, Terraform, IAM, Prometheus, OPA, ArgoCD
example.outcome: you can see why load must be managed.

check.q: Why has developer cognitive load increased so much?
check.a: Developers are now expected to handle a large and growing infrastructure and operations stack as well as their domain code.

conways-law-and-the-reverse-conway-maneu.core: Systems mirror the communication structures of their organisations (Conway's Law), so to get a desired architecture you design team boundaries to match it: the Reverse (Inverse) Conway Maneuver.

first_principles.problem: Functional teams (frontend, backend, ops) produce layered architectures where every feature needs coordination across all of them.
truths: Team design is an architectural tool.

analogy.title: Roads following neighbourhood boundaries
analogy.story: Plan neighbourhoods to get the road network you want.
analogy.breaks: Reorgs are disruptive, so change team structure deliberately and incrementally.

example.title: Realigning teams to domains
example.outcome: org structure as an architecture lever.

check.q: What is the Reverse Conway Maneuver?
check.a: Designing team structures to match the system architecture you want, so the architecture emerges from the organisation.

the-four-team-types.core: Team Topologies defines four team types: stream-aligned (delivers value for a domain or user journey), platform (internal self-service products), enabling (coaches teams in new capabilities) and complicated-subsystem (owns deep specialist components). Every team should clearly be one of them.

first_principles.problem: Ambiguous team purposes ('the DevOps team', 'the integration team') create confusion and hidden dependencies.
truths: Most value comes from stream-aligned teams.
Supporting types exist to help them.

analogy.title: Roles in a hospital
analogy.story: Ward teams treat patients (stream-aligned), facilities and labs support them (platform), trainers upskill staff (enabling) and specialists handle rare procedures (complicated subsystem).
analogy.breaks: Real teams sometimes blend types temporarily, so aim for clarity over purity.

example.title: Typing an organisation
example.outcome: a shared vocabulary for team design.

check.q: Which team type exists mainly to support stream-aligned teams with self-service capabilities?

the-stream-aligned-team-the-value-creato.core: Stream-aligned teams own a flow of change for a product, user journey or domain end to end: build, deploy, run and learn. Everything else in the organisation exists to help them deliver quickly and independently.

first_principles.problem: Teams that can't deploy or change their own systems without others wait in handoffs and lose ownership.
derivation: Align to a **value stream** (journey or domain).
Size them at **5–9 people** to keep load manageable.

analogy.title: A food truck crew
analogy.story: They own the whole experience, from cooking to serving to cleaning up, and can change the menu daily.
analogy.breaks: Full end-to-end ownership can overload teams without platform support.

example.title: A checkout team
flow: Owns checkout UI, API, payments integration
example.outcome: teams that deliver value end to end.

check.a: It owns a flow of value (product, journey or domain) end to end, with the autonomy to deliver independently.

the-platform-team-reducing-the-load.core: Platform teams build the paved roads: self-service internal products (deploy, provision, observe, secure) that make the right thing the easy thing, measured by how much load they remove from stream-aligned teams.

first_principles.problem: Each stream team builds its own CI, monitoring and infrastructure differently, duplicating effort and multiplying load.
truths: Shared needs are best served centrally.

analogy.title: A city's utilities department
analogy.story: Residents get water and power without building their own wells and generators.
analogy.breaks: Platforms that become gatekeepers recreate bottlenecks, so self-service is essential.

example.title: A platform capability
flow: Stream teams each ran their own Prometheus
Platform offers managed metrics + default dashboards
example.outcome: stream teams freed to focus on value.

check.q: What's the platform team's main success measure?
check.a: How much it reduces stream-aligned teams' cognitive load and how widely its capabilities are adopted.

the-enabling-complicated-subsystem-teams.core: Enabling teams are coaches who help stream teams adopt new capabilities (testing, observability, security) and then step away. Complicated-subsystem teams own components that need deep specialist knowledge (codecs, ML models, trading engines), so stream teams don't have to.

first_principles.problem: Stream teams struggle to adopt practices they don't know, or are burdened with highly specialised components.
truths: Some knowledge is too specialised to distribute.
derivation: **Enabling**: time-boxed engagements, facilitating mode, build capability and leave.
**Complicated subsystem**: an encapsulated specialist component with a clear interface.
Avoid enabling teams turning into **permanent dependencies**.

analogy.title: A driving instructor vs. a specialist mechanic
analogy.story: The instructor teaches you to drive and then leaves; the mechanic handles the turbocharger you'll never learn to fix.
analogy.breaks: Enabling teams are often mistaken for gatekeepers or doers, so define their mode clearly.

example.title: An enabling engagement
flow: Enabling team joins Checkout for 6 weeks
Pairs on contract tests + CI gates

check.q: How does an enabling team differ from a platform team?
check.a: Enabling teams coach stream teams temporarily to build capability; platform teams provide ongoing self-service products.

interaction-modes-how-teams-talk-to-each.core: Three interaction modes: Collaboration (working closely and temporarily to discover something new), X-as-a-Service (consuming a well-defined offering with minimal interaction) and Facilitating (helping another team learn). Choose the mode explicitly and evolve it.

first_principles.problem: Platform and stream teams collaborate on everything forever, so meetings multiply and neither team moves fast.
truths: Collaboration costs time but speeds discovery.
derivation: Declare the **mode** for each team pair.

analogy.title: How you work with a contractor
analogy.story: Co-designing a renovation (collaboration), buying from a catalogue (service), or being taught DIY (facilitating).
analogy.breaks: Mismatched assumptions about the mode create friction, so write them down.

example.title: Modes changing over time
flow: Platform + Payments collaborate on secrets rotation (Q1)
Enabling team facilitates other teams' adoption (Q3)

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Coordination cost falls as the capability matures.

check.q: When should a team interaction move from Collaboration to X-as-a-Service?
check.a: Once the capability is understood and stable enough to be consumed through a clear interface.

thinnest-viable-platform-tvp-just-enough.core: Platform teams are tempted to build comprehensive enterprise platforms up front. The TVP is the smallest platform that meaningfully reduces stream teams' load (possibly just documentation, conventions and a few templates), grown according to demand.

first_principles.problem: A new platform team disappears for a year building everything, and stream teams solve their own problems in the meantime.
derivation: Keep the platform **as thin as possible**.

analogy.title: A minimum viable product
analogy.story: Ship the simplest useful version, then learn what to add.
analogy.breaks: Being thin doesn't excuse being unreliable. What you ship must be solid.

example.title: A TVP progression
example.outcome: platforms that grow with real needs.

check.q: Why start with a Thinnest Viable Platform?
check.a: It delivers value quickly, builds trust and lets real demand guide further investment, avoiding overbuilding.

measuring-cognitive-load-how-do-you-know.core: Cognitive load is invisible, so measure proxies: team surveys (confidence across owned systems), the number of services, technologies and on-call scopes per team, time spent on non-domain work, onboarding time and incident patterns.

first_principles.problem: Leaders keep adding responsibilities to teams because nobody can show they're overloaded.
derivation: **Survey**: 'How well do you understand the systems you own?' (1–5).
**Count** services, languages and tools per team.
**Track** time on infra vs domain work.
**Watch** onboarding time and incidents caused by unfamiliarity.

analogy.title: A load gauge on a truck
analogy.story: You can't see the strain on the axle, but a gauge warns you before it breaks.
analogy.breaks: Surveys can be biased, so combine them with objective proxies.

example.title: A load assessment
flow: Action: platform takes infra; split domain

check.q: Name two proxies for measuring a team's cognitive load.
check.a: For example, the number of services and technologies owned, and the share of time spent on non-domain infrastructure work (plus survey confidence).
